opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think my view has shifted quite a bit. A few years ago, I would have told you, along with a lot of people in the field, that there's a fundamental ceiling on what you can learn from text alone. The argument went something like this: language is a system of symbols, and the meaning of those symbols comes from their connection to the world: to perception, to action, to the things people are actually talking about. If all you ever see is the symbols, then you're doing something like learning the shape of a dictionary where every definition points to other words, and you never get out of that loop.

What changed for me was partly empirical and partly conceptual. On the empirical side, we started seeing language models do things that are hard to explain unless they're representing something about the situations the text describes. Some of our own work, and work from other groups, probed these models and found internal representations that track the state of the world being described. When you read a text-based game or a story about objects being moved between containers, the model's hidden states seem to encode which object is where, and you can intervene on those representations and change the model's predictions in the way you'd expect. That looks a lot more like a world model than like surface co-occurrence statistics.

On the conceptual side, I came to appreciate that text isn't some ungrounded floating thing. Text is produced by people who are grounded, who are looking at the world, acting in it, and trying to communicate about it. So the structure of the world leaves an imprint on the distribution of text. If you model that distribution well enough, you're forced, at least in part, to model the processes that generated it, and those include people's beliefs, goals, and the states of the world they're describing. The grounding is sort of there indirectly, mediated through the authors.

That said, I don't think I've flipped all the way to the view that text is sufficient for everything. There are clearly gaps. Models learn some things from text very inefficiently, or get them wrong in systematic ways: fine-grained spatial and physical reasoning, perceptual properties, things people rarely bother to write down because they're obvious to anyone with a body. And there's a difference between having representations that are in principle related to the world and being able to reliably use them, update them when things change, or connect them to new perceptual input. So my current view is that "can you learn anything about meaning from text alone?" has the answer "yes, a surprising amount," and the more interesting question now is *what* you can and can't learn, how efficiently, and where explicit grounding in perception and interaction gives you something you couldn't easily get otherwise. That's a much more nuanced and, honestly, more fun research question than the yes-or-no version we were arguing about before.

r001.rationale: The response describes an earlier belief in a ceiling on learning from text, but does not tie it to model or algorithm capabilities around 2012–2014.

r002.rationale: It credits empirical findings and the insight that grounded authors leave traces in text, but does not say Andreas had underestimated what internet-scale corpora could teach.

r003.rationale: It asks what can and cannot be learned from text, but does not identify the specific unresolved comparison between human-scale and internet-scale corpora.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think my view has shifted quite a bit, and honestly in a direction I didn't expect when I started working on this.

If you'd asked me around 2017 or 2018, I would have told you pretty confidently that grounding was necessary. I'd spent a lot of my PhD on instruction following, on models that had to connect language to actions in an environment, and the whole premise of that work was that meaning lives in the relationship between words and the world. Text alone, on that view, is just a record of other people talking about a world the model never gets to see. You can learn a lot of statistics about which words go together, but it's not clear why that should bottom out in anything we'd want to call understanding. Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made that argument very sharply in the "octopus" paper, and I was broadly sympathetic to it.

What changed is partly empirical and partly a shift in how I think about the question itself. On the empirical side, the thing that really got my attention wasn't the headline benchmark numbers. It was looking inside models. When we and others started probing what language models represent, we kept finding things that looked a lot like world models. You train a model on transcripts of Othello games and it builds an internal representation of the board. You train on text about entities and you can find representations that track where things are, what state they're in, whether a proposition is currently true or false in the discourse. Nobody told the model to build those structures. They emerged because predicting the next token well is easier if you have a compressed model of the situation that generated the text.

That pushed me toward thinking that the text-versus-grounding distinction was a bit of a false dichotomy. Text isn't an unstructured signal. It's produced by agents who are themselves grounded, who have beliefs and goals and perceptual access to the world, and a huge amount of that structure leaks into the statistics of what they write. So a model trained on text is doing something like inferring the latent variables, the world states and the intentions, that would explain why people said what they said. That's a form of grounding, just mediated through other people rather than through the model's own sensors.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think the strong form of my old view was simply wrong. There are things text-only models are clearly bad at. Their world models are patchy and inconsistent. They'll represent a fact correctly in one context and contradict it in another. And there's a category of knowledge, like fine-grained spatial reasoning or physical intuitions about how objects behave, where the coverage in text is thin because humans don't bother to write it down. We don't write "the cup did not pass through the table" very often. So I think explicit grounding still matters, but the role I'd assign it now is more about calibrating and filling gaps than about being the thing that makes understanding possible at all.

The other thing I'd say is that the question "does it understand" has become less interesting to me than more concrete questions. Does the model have a representation of this situation? Can I read it out? Can I intervene on it and change the behavior in the way I'd predict? Those are questions you can actually answer, and when you answer them, the yes-or-no debate about understanding kind of dissolves into a bunch of specific findings about what's there and what isn't. So I'd say I've gone from being a skeptic about text-only learning to being someone who thinks the interesting work is characterizing exactly what kind of world model you get from it, where it breaks, and what the cheapest way to patch the holes is.

r001.rationale: The response places Andreas’s earlier view around 2017–2018 and links it to his PhD work; it does not attribute that view to the capabilities of models and algorithms available around 2012–2014.

r002.rationale: The response says probing models revealed world-like representations, but does not attribute his revision to underestimating what internet-scale text corpora could teach.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise the question of whether human-scale text can yield the world understanding available from internet-scale corpora.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become much less confident that explicit grounding is necessary. There’s a very reasonable argument that language is just symbols, and unless you connect those symbols to perception or action, you can’t learn what they mean. But language is produced by people who are interacting with the world, and that leaves a lot of structure in the text. You can potentially recover quite a bit about the world by learning to model that structure.

The question, then, is what kind of understanding you’re talking about. Learning how objects relate to one another, or what tends to cause what, seems increasingly possible from text alone. That doesn’t automatically give you the ability to recognize those objects in an image or manipulate them. Those are additional capabilities that need some connection to perception and action.

So I’ve moved away from the idea that grounding is a prerequisite for any meaningful understanding, toward asking which aspects of understanding text can support and which aspects require other kinds of experience. I don’t think we have a clean boundary there yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a change in stance but does not connect the earlier belief to model or learning algorithm capabilities around 2012–2014.

r002.rationale: It says text contains structure that can support learning about the world, but does not attribute the revision to underestimating what internet-scale text corpora could teach.

r003.rationale: The candidate says there is no clean boundary between what text and other experience can support, but does not raise the question of human-scale versus internet-scale text corpora.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become less convinced that explicit grounding is a prerequisite for learning something meaningful about the world. Text isn’t disconnected from the world: people produce it based on their experiences, and a lot of that structure ends up reflected in what they say. So even a system that only observes text can, in principle, recover some of the structure that generated it.

The harder question is what it can’t recover. There may be distinctions that simply aren’t expressed in the data, or things that are much easier to learn by acting and observing the consequences. And being able to answer questions about something isn’t necessarily the same as being able to interact with it successfully.

So I’ve moved away from thinking of grounding as a binary requirement for understanding. I’m more interested now in which aspects of the world you can learn from language, which require other kinds of experience, and how we can design experiments that tell those apart.

r001.rationale: The response says his view changed, but does not mention model or algorithm capabilities available around 2012–2014 as the reason for his earlier belief.

r002.rationale: It says text reflects the world and can convey some of its structure, but does not attribute his revision to underestimating what internet-scale text corpora could teach.

r003.rationale: The response discusses what language can and cannot teach, but does not raise the specific comparison between human-scale and internet-scale text corpora.
